title: Do Not Resuscitate
lines: PLEASANT VALLEY FIRE DEPARTMENT EMS PROTOCOLS
Outside the hospital Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) requests are orders by a patient’s physician to refrain from initiating
cardiopulmonary resuscitative measures in the event of a cardiac or respiratory arrest. DNR requests are compatible
with maximal therapeutic care and the patient may receive vigorous support (i.e. IV’s & drugs) until the point of cardiac
The EMS provider will honor the DNR request when properly executed and presented. Guidelines for acceptance of DNR
1. If any doubt exists about the validity of the DNR form or the intent of the patient or the appropriate surrogate,
resuscitation must be initiated and MEDICAL CONTROL CONTACTED.
2. The patient must not be pregnant
3. Alternately worded directives to limit care, (i.e. Supportive Care Only, Limited Terminal Care, Justified Use of
Conservative Care) are not acceptable substitutes for DNR directives. If presented with an alternate form,
4. The DNR form must be signed and dated by the patient or appropriate surrogate, the witness, and the patient’s
5. The revocation provision must remain unsigned in order for this DNR form to remain valid.
6. The DNR form must be with the patient at the time of the EMS providers’ arrival.
7. The form must be an original and seen by the EMS provider.
8. No cardiac monitoring is necessary. No Medical Control contact is necessary.
9. If a DNR Request Form is presented after BLS or ALS resuscitative procedures (including the AED) have begun,
The EMS report shall include the existence of a DNR and the DNR request form number. If a copy can be obtained it shall
be attached to the EMS report. The original DNR form shall remain at the facility or home. If the patient is transported,
the DNR form will accompany the patient.

Purpose: The purpose of this policy is to assist EMS personnel with clear rules for managing situations in which the
patient or the patient’s representative refuses care or transportation by EMS.
Right to Refuse: An adult patient who is conscious, mentally competent, and understands the consequences of his or
her decision has the right to refuse are or transportation by EMS. A patient that refuses treatment or transport must be
offered treatment or transport and advised of the benefits of treatment or transport and the specific risks of refusing
treatment or transport. The offer of treatment or transport and description of the risks of refusal should be
documented in the trip sheet and on the Refusal Form.
No Right to Refuse: Conversely, where a patient is a minor or otherwise not competent, or unable to understand the
consequences of his or her decision, the patient may not refuse treatment or transport for himself, and EMS may have
implied consent to treat or transport. In this situation, EMS must contact Medical Control for directions regarding
treatment and transport (Mandatory Medical Control Contact).
Mandatory Medical Control Contact: Medical Control contact is mandatory if the crew believes that the patient may be
at significant harm to him or herself by refusing treatment or transport. The crew may contact Medical Control at any
time there is a question in regards to the patient condition. Utilization of the EMS radio is mandatory if communication
allows. The purpose of mandatory Medical Control Contact is to:
1. Assist the paramedic in persuading a reluctant patient to be transported. Occasionally, a recommendation from
a physician may be all that is needed to facilitate transport.
2. Serve to support the paramedic’s judgment that the patient is acting against medical advice.
1. Patient: Any person who is ill or injured or in need of treatment by medical personnel. This includes any person
that has activated the EMS system or for whom the EMS system has been activated, including emergency and
non-emergency calls for service, or any person that presents himself to EMS personnel with a medically related
complaint such that it could be reasonable inferred that the person is seeking or in need of medical attention.
2. Not a Patient: A person who is not ill or injured or in need of treatment by medical personnel. This includes
individuals who may have been involved in a situation that either did result or could have resulted in the

title: Suspected Abuse/Neglect Policy
lines: PLEASANT VALLEY FIRE DEPARTMENT EMS PROTOCOLS
Definition – Includes physical, emotional, or sexual abuse as well as physical or emotional neglect.
1. State law requires that suspected child abuse or neglect be reported to the Missouri Department of Health and
Senior Services. Any Paramedic, EMT, or First Responder having reasonable cause to suspect that a child (any
person less than 18 years of age) has been or may be abused or neglected must report or cause a report to be
made to the Division of Family Services. Notification should be done by telephoning 1-800-392-3738
2. State law requires that suspected elder abuse or neglect be reported to the Missouri Department of Health and
Senior Services. Any Paramedic, EMT, or First Responder having reasonable cause to suspect that a person sixty
years of age or older (or handicapped person between the ages of 18 and 59) has been or may be abuse or
neglected must report or cause a report to be made to the Department of Health and Senior Services.
Notification should be done by telephoning 1-800-392-0210
a. Notification of suspected elder abuse or neglect may also be made at the State of Missouri website at
Provide necessary medical care according to the appropriate protocol.
Although a preliminary assessment of abuse or neglect is made in the field, appropriate personnel make the final
determination upon review of the incident. Accusations of abuse or neglect should not be made in the field.
In a private and confidential environment notify the nurse and/or physician at the receiving hospital of the facts upon
which neglect of abuse is suspected.
Notification of the Assistant Chief of EMS of the facts of the neglect or abuse is encouraged.
The following information shall be included in the attending paramedics report:
1. All facts upon which abuse or neglect is suspected.
2. Identity of nurse and/or physician notified.
3. Whether physician or hospital staff is going to make proper notification.
4. If notification is made by the attending paramedic.

lines: PLEASANT VALLEY FIRE DEPARTMENT EMS PROTOCOLS

This protocol in intended to provide guidelines for care of patients following the use of TASER type weapons by law
enforcement. For situations involving level of consciousness, significant trauma, and/or other medical problems, follow
There have been reports of death involving the use of a TASER weapon on combative patients. These deaths may be
associated with agitated delirium, hyperdynamic (adrenergic) drugs particularly cocaine, methamphetamine and
phencyclidine, and hyperthermia as major co-morbid factors. Therefore, it is imperative that these patients receive a
thorough assessment for these risk factors, and are not restrained in an improper position. If a patient remains
combative, follow the Patient Restraint Procedure.
Assure the scene is secure. Use of this type of weapon to subdue a violent person implies they were a risk to
themselves or others. Do not enter scene until advised to do so by law enforcement personnel

o Darts in other locations may be carefully removed
o ESTABLISH IV ACCESS AS INDICATED BY OTHER SYMPTOMS OR APPROPRIATE PROTOCOLS
o Place one hand on the patient in the area where the dart is embedded and stabilize the skin surrounding
the puncture site. Firmly grasp the dart with the other hand
o In one fluid motion, pull the dart straight out from the puncture site
o Assure the dart is intact and no portion of the dart remains inside the patient’s skin
o Removed darts should be handled like contaminated sharps

lines: PLEASANT VALLEY FIRE DEPARTMENT EMS PROTOCOLS
INDICATIONS: Extremity wounds where direct pressure with a sterile dressing alone does not control active bleeding
CONTRAINDICATIONS: Do not place around the neck
PRECAUTIONS: Do not place directly over a wound
1. Expose the wound and place the wounded extremity through the loop of the Omni-Tape band. The CAT will
normally be 2-4 inches above the injury.
2. Pull the free end of the Omni-Tape band tight and secure it back onto itself using the Velcro.
3. Do not secure the band past the windlass clip.
4. Twist the windlass rob until bright red bleeding stops
5. Secure the rod by inserting it into the windlass clip.
6. Small extremities will allow you to extend the Omni-Tape band over the top of the windlass rod and clip.
7. Pull the Velcro windlass strap tight over the windlass clip and Omni-Tape band.
8. Mark the patient’s head with the letter “T” and annotate the date/time/location of the CAT on the field medical
Card. Patient is now ready for transport unless further medical assessment is required.
9. Never remove or cover a tourniquet and only use on a leg or arm.

title: Patient Restraint
lines: PLEASANT VALLEY FIRE DEPARTMENT EMS PROTOCOLS
The purpose of this policy is to set forth principles and procedures for the prehospital patient restraint (PPR) of persons
at risk for harm to self or others, including emergency medical services personnel.
The safety of EMS personnel is paramount for the consideration, initiation, and application of PPR. Also, the protection
of patients from self-harm or harm to others while maintaining patient dignity to the greatest extent possible while
utilizing the least restrictive method of restraint appropriate to the situation.
This policy applies to all patients whom have demonstrated violence toward self or others, or there is reason to believe
that combative or violent behavior is imminent, through actions or verbalizations by the patient or reasonable layperson
1. All patients who are demonstrating physical harm to self or others including, but not limited to, evidence of
suicidal or homicidal behavior, by act or verbalization.
2. All patients demonstrating decreased ability to care for self as evidence by, but not limited to, cognitive
impairment or suspected intoxication leading to exposure of self or others to potentially limb or life-threatening
3. Patient with altered mental status leading to decreased capacity to understand situation and circumstances of
their current medical condition resulting in aggressive or combative behavior towards emergency personnel.
4. Patients in custody of law enforcement or under involuntary detention.
1. Do not restrain the patient in the prone position
1. Always assure access to patient’s airway should airway management be needed
2. Always assure access to extremities should vascular access be needed
1. When at all possible, the patient should be approached in a calm, non-threatening and supporting manner.
Verbal de-escalation efforts should be attempted unless there is imminent danger to patient or bystanders. If
the EMS personnel believe that their personal safety is at risk, law enforcement should be contacted for
2. When imminent danger to the patient or others is identified, a unified, multiple emergency personnel approach
should be made to gain control of the patient. Placement of physical restraints, including approved hood with
spit shield, approved soft wrist and ankle restraints should be considered first. Progressive restraint beginning
with wrists, then ankles, to immobilization on long spine board should be determined to provide the least
amount of restraint necessary to accomplish protection of crew and patient.
3. Hard extremity restraints including handcuffs and shackles should be used only when other methods fail or
unusable due to circumstances and efforts to replace with approved restraints made.
4. If handcuffs or shackles are used, they should only be placed by appropriate law enforcement personnel and
when law enforcement will travel with the patient or in immediate vicinity of the ambulance. EMS personnel
should always have available, the means to immediately remove restraints.
5. Patients under arrest shall be thoroughly searched by law enforcement prior to being placed into any
ambulance. Law enforcement agencies retain the responsibility for safe transport of patients under arrest or
6. Patients should be restrained in a supine position and immobilized on a long spine board whenever possible. It
is never appropriate to “sandwich” patient between boards, or to “hog-tie” in any fashion a patient for transport
by EMS. Any restraint placed should not compromise normal respiratory efforts or circulation.
7. Vital signs and patient monitoring should be accomplished as soon as possible after placement of appropriate
restraints. Potential causes of the behavior, including hypoxemia and hypoglycemia, should be considered and
efforts to identify and manage as soon as possible.
8. ONCE PHYSICAL RESTRAINTS ARE IN PLACE, CHEMICAL RESTRAINT SHOULD BE STRONGLY CONSIDERED AND
ADMINISTERED IF THE PATIENT CONTINUES TO EXHIBIT BEHAVIOR IN RESTRAINTS THAT COULD HARM SELF
OR OTHERS. CHEMICAL RESTRAINT SHOULD ONLY BE UTILITZED WHEN THE PATIENT CAN BE ADEQUATELY
AND CONTINUOUSLY MONITORED BY THE PARAMEDIC. REFER TO COMBINED BEHAVIORAL/PSYCHIATRIC
9. Once restrained, the patient should be isolated and placed into the ambulance as soon as possible and
transported to the closest appropriate facility as per the Determination of Hospital Destination Policy.
10. Physical restraints should be reassessed at a minimum of every ten minutes during transport for the first hour,
and every thirty minutes thereafter. The restrained extremities should be assessed for neurovascular function
11. Always considered consultation with on-line medical control for questions or assistance in determining the most
appropriate restraint method for any situation. Patients with medical conditions that appear to compromise
their ability to consent for or decline care may be restrained as necessary and transported without law
enforcement authority in situations in which a life-threatening emergency exists or potentially exists. Medical
control should be contacted in all instances where patients are transported against their consent unless under
arrest or duly exercised involuntary detention.

3. Complete vital signs including pulse oximetry initially and at hospital arrival at a minimum
5. Detailed description of patient injuries and any bystander injuries
